summary.text: A finite covering check for every \(1\le d\le2025\) finds primes \(p,q\) with different final digits such that \(pq\le150\) and \(\gcd(pq,d)=1\). Multiplication by \(d\) permutes residues modulo \(pq\), so some index \(0\le i<pq\le150\) makes \(pq\mid a+id\), forcing that term to have the differently ending prime divisors \(p\) and \(q\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
We prove that the asserted arithmetic progression cannot exist.

Call a positive integer lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same final decimal digit. Equivalently, if
\[
R(n)=\{p\bmod 10:p\text{ is a prime divisor of }n\},
\]
then lopsidedness is the condition \(|R(n)|\le 1\). (For the progression in question every term is at least 2, so there is no issue concerning the vacuous condition for 0 or 1.)

We first establish the number-theoretic covering fact that drives the argument.

**Lemma 1.** For every integer \(d\) with \(1\le d\le 2025\), there are primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
p\not\equiv q\pmod {10},\qquad pq\le 150,
\qquad\text{and}\qquad \gcd(pq,d)=1.
\]

**Proof.** Consider the five primes
\[
B=\{2,3,5,7,11\}.
\]
Their final decimal digits are respectively \(2,3,5,7,1\), so any two distinct members of \(B\) have different final digits. Moreover, the product of any two of them is at most \(7\cdot 11=77<150\).

If at least two primes in \(B\) do not divide \(d\), choose two such primes as \(p,q\). Since they are prime and neither divides \(d\), their product is coprime to \(d\), and all the other required properties follow from the preceding observations.

It remains to consider the possibility that at most one member of \(B\) fails to divide \(d\). It is impossible that every member of \(B\) divides \(d\), because they are distinct primes and hence their product would divide \(d\), whereas
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310>2025\ge d.
\]
Thus exactly one member \(r\) of \(B\) does not divide \(d\), and all the other four do divide \(d\).

For each possible value of \(r\), choose an auxiliary prime \(s\) as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
r&2&3&5&7&11\\ \hline
s&13&17&13&13&13.
\end{array}
\]
In every column, \(r\) and \(s\) have different final digits, and their products are respectively
\[
26,\ 51,\ 65,\ 91,\ 143,
\]
all at most 150.

We claim that the chosen \(s\) cannot divide \(d\). Indeed, if it did, then the four members of \(B\setminus\{r\}\), together with \(s\), would all be distinct prime divisors of \(d\). Their product would therefore divide \(d\). For the five possibilities for \(r\), those products are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
r&2&3&5&7&11\\ \hline
\left(\prod_{t\in B\setminus\{r\}}t\right)s
&1155\cdot13&770\cdot17&462\cdot13&330\cdot13&210\cdot13\\
&15015&13090&6006&4290&2730.
\end{array}
\]
Every one is greater than 2025, contradicting the fact that it divides the positive integer \(d\le2025\). Consequently neither \(r\) nor \(s\) divides \(d\). Since both are prime, \(\gcd(rs,d)=1\). Taking \(p=r\) and \(q=s\) proves the lemma. \(\square\)

The second ingredient says that a sufficiently short initial segment of an arithmetic progression must contain a multiple of every small modulus coprime to its difference.

**Lemma 2.** Let \(a,d,m\) be integers with \(m\ge1\), \(m\le150\), and \(\gcd(m,d)=1\). Then there is an integer \(i\) satisfying
\[
0\le i<150
\]
such that
\[
m\mid a+id.
\]

**Proof.** Because \(d\) is invertible modulo \(m\), the congruence
\[
id\equiv-a\pmod m
\]
has a solution, namely
\[
i\equiv-a d^{-1}\pmod m.
\]
Choose its least nonnegative representative. Then \(0\le i<m\le150\), and the defining congruence says exactly that \(m\mid a+id\). \(\square\)

We now negate the conjecture. Suppose, for contradiction, that there are integers \(a,d\) with
\[
a\ge2,\qquad 1\le d\le2025,
\]
such that every one of the 150 terms
\[
a,
\ a+d,
\ a+2d,
\ldots,
\ a+149d
\]
is lopsided.

Apply Lemma 1 to this \(d\). We obtain primes \(p,q\) for which
\[
p\not\equiv q\pmod {10},
\qquad pq\le150,
\qquad \gcd(pq,d)=1.
\]
Set \(m=pq\). Since \(m\ge1\), Lemma 2 supplies an index \(i\) with
\[
0\le i<150
\quad\text{and}\quad
pq\mid a+id.
\]
Thus both \(p\) and \(q\) divide the progression term
\[
n=a+id.
\]
This term is positive—in fact \(n\ge a\ge2\)—so \(p\) and \(q\) genuinely occur among its prime divisors. Their final decimal digits are different. Hence the set
\[
R(n)=\{\ell\bmod10:\ell\text{ is a prime divisor of }n\}
\]
contains the two distinct elements \(p\bmod10\) and \(q\bmod10\), and therefore \(|R(n)|\ge2\). The number \(n=a+id\) is not lopsided.

But \(0\le i<150\), so \(n\) is one of the 150 terms that were assumed all to be lopsided. This contradiction proves that no such \(a,d\) exist. Therefore the claimed existence of a 150-term increasing arithmetic progression with starting term at least 2 and difference at most 2025, all of whose terms belong to A381159, is false.
